finding.claim: /admin/drop never enforces its dba role check: the Authorize() error is discarded, so any caller who reaches the handler with a context user runs the DROP.
finding.source: HTTP request to /admin/drop (route registered at api.go:44); caller identity comes from the request context via userFrom (api.go:25).
finding.sink: runSQL("DROP TABLE " + ...) at api.go:27 (destructive statement executed unconditionally).

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered directly with dropTable; no auth middleware is attached in this file.
u := userFrom(r) reads the *User from the request context. Its population is not visible in this directory.
Authorize(u, "dba") is called as a bare statement; its error return is ignored.
Execution continues to runSQL regardless of the authorization outcome.

finding.guards_checked: Authorize() (api.go:13-20) correctly returns an error for non-dba users, but the handler discards it. No early return, no middleware in this file, no route-level guard. vacuum (api.go:31-39) does check the error, which shows the intended pattern. Precondition: the upstream code that sets the "user" context value must admit the attacker. If it does not, userFrom panics before any SQL runs. I could not verify that middleware from this directory.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize() (api.go:13-20) does return an error for non-dba users, but its result is discarded by the bare call at api.go:26, so it is not effective. No early return follows it, and no middleware or route guard wraps /admin/drop (api.go:44-45, registered directly on the default mux). The vacuum handler (api.go:33-36) checks the error, which confirms the intended pattern.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate and the missing check is real (api.go:26 discards Authorize's error, and api.go:27 runs the DROP unconditionally), but whether an attacker can reach it depends on the "user" context value being set by upstream code that is not in this directory (api.go:22 would panic on a nil context value, so nothing in this file reaches line 27 by itself), and I cannot verify what role that upstream auth admits.

finding.claim: The table name for /admin/drop is built by concatenating the raw form value into a SQL string, enabling arbitrary SQL injection, including stacked statements.
finding.source: r.FormValue("t") at api.go:27, from the attacker-controlled query string or form body of POST /admin/drop.
finding.sink: runSQL at api.go:27, which receives the concatenated SQL string.

trace.note: Route /admin/drop is reachable by the caller.
r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into "DROP TABLE " with no allowlist, quoting, or parameterization.
The resulting string is passed to runSQL. Its body is an empty stub here, so the real driver behaviour depends on the implementation that is not in this directory.

finding.guards_checked: No input validation, allowlist, identifier quoting, or prepared statement. Table identifiers cannot be bound as parameters, so an allowlist of permitted table names is the required control. The only guard is the authorization in SEC-1, which is not enforced. Precondition: the caller must reach the handler, which SEC-1 shows is possible for any authenticated caller. Impact: arbitrary destructive SQL, including dropping any table, or injected statements if the driver accepts multiple statements.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is a bare call whose error return is discarded, so the handler proceeds regardless. No allowlist, identifier quoting, or parameterization exists at api.go:27.
verdict.reason: At api.go:27, r.FormValue("t") is concatenated directly into "DROP TABLE " and passed to runSQL, and the route is registered at api.go:44; the only authorization check at api.go:26 discards its error, so any caller that reaches dropTable (only a request context with a user is needed, since userFrom at api.go:22 panics without one) can inject arbitrary SQL. The runSQL body is a stub, so the stacked-statement part depends on the real driver, but the injectable identifier is confirmed by the code shown.
